## Introduction

This tutorial covers key concepts from [Chapter 7: Data Import](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html), [Chapter 5: Data Tidying](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html), and [Chapter 9: Layers](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html) from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

You will use AI to analyze a year of Billboard Hot 100 chart rankings. Your job is to steer the analysis, render often, inspect the output, and decide what the data can honestly show.

###

Use AI however you like. The rhythm is always the same: describe the result you want, let the agent edit your files, review its changes, render, and inspect the output.

###

A CSV is the plainest possible table: one line per row, values separated by commas, and a first line naming the columns. Here are the first lines of the file you will download, cut off after five columns:

```{.output}
artist,track,date.entered,wk1,wk2
2 Pac,Baby Don't Cry (Keep...,2000-02-26,87,82
2Ge+her,The Hardest Part Of ...,2000-09-02,91,87
```

No types, no formulas, no formatting — which is exactly why every programming language, database, and spreadsheet program can read one.

## Billboard Hot 100

[Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/) has published the Hot 100 every week since August 1958. The file you are about to download covers one year of it: one row per song, with the song's rank in each week after it entered the chart.

###

`billboard.csv` is about 85 KB: 317 rows, one per song, and 79 columns — the artist, the track, the date it entered the chart, and its rank in each of the next 76 weeks. Most of the week cells hold `NA`, because few songs stay on the chart for more than a few months.

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +

### Exercise 9

Create a small table showing how many rankings are missing and present for `wk1`, `wk4`, `wk10`, `wk20`, `wk40`, and `wk76`. Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create a small table showing how many rankings are missing and present for wk1, wk4, wk10, wk20, wk40, and wk76. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-6-answer
#| echo: true
billboard |>
  summarise(
    wk1 = sum(is.na(wk1)),
    wk4 = sum(is.na(wk4)),
    wk10 = sum(is.na(wk10)),
    wk20 = sum(is.na(wk20)),
    wk40 = sum(is.na(wk40)),
    wk76 = sum(is.na(wk76))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "missing"
  ) |>
  mutate(present = nrow(billboard) - missing)
```

###

`wk1` has no missing rankings because every song is on the chart in its first week, while later weeks have more missing values because songs drop off the Hot 100. Of the 280 songs still charting in week 6, 251 had improved on their week-1 rank, so the chart is thinning out and the survivors are rising at the same time.

### Exercise 10

Reshape `billboard` so the week columns become two columns, `week` and `rank`, then plot each song's ranking over time. Update your working chunk, render, and inspect the plot in the rendered HTML.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Reshape billboard so the week columns become two columns, week and rank, then plot each song's ranking over time. Update your working chunk, render, and inspect the plot in the rendered HTML. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-8-answer
#| echo: true
billboard |>
  mutate(song = str_c(artist, " - ", track)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = rank, group = song)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.18, color = "gray50") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "Billboard rankings over time",
    subtitle = "Each line is one song after it entered the Hot 100",
    x = "Weeks since entering the chart",
    y = "Billboard rank",
    caption = "Source: tidyr::billboard"
  )
```

###

Notice that most lines stop at week 20. The chart holds 146 of these songs in week 20 and only 65 in week 21 — a cliff that none of the summaries so far gave any hint of.

### Exercise 11

Count the songs whose last week on the chart is exactly week 20, and how many of those were ranked below 50 in that week. Update your working chunk, render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-18
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Count the songs whose last week on the chart is exactly week 20, and how many of those were ranked below 50 in that week. Update your working chunk, render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-18-answer
#| echo: true
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  group_by(artist, track) |>
  slice_max(week, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(week == 20) |>
  summarise(
    songs_ending_week_20 = n(),
    ranked_below_50 = sum(rank > 50)
  )
```

###

Billboard has a *recurrent* rule: a song that has been on the Hot 100 for 20 weeks and has fallen below #50 is removed from the chart, however steadily it is still selling. That rule, not a sudden loss of popularity, is why the lines stop in a cliff at week 20 rather than tapering off.

### Exercise 12

The full trajectory plot is useful, but it is too dense to explain individual stories. Focus on songs that reached the top 10 and look for different kinds of hit trajectories.

Create a song-level summary with each song's first rank, best rank, first week at its best rank, and total weeks on the chart. Then identify three notable top-10 songs: the fastest song to reach number one, the slowest song to reach number one, and the top-10 song with the longest chart run. Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Create a song-level summary with each song's first rank, best rank, first week at its best rank, and total weeks on the chart. Then identify three notable top-10 songs: the fastest song to reach number one, the slowest song to reach number one, and the top-10 song with the longest chart run. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-10-answer
#| echo: true
billboard_song_summary <- billboard |>
  mutate(song = str_c(artist, " - ", track)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  group_by(artist, track, song) |>
  summarise(
    first_rank = rank[week == min(week)][1],
    best_rank = min(rank),
    first_best_week = min(week[rank == best_rank]),
    weeks_on_chart = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bind_rows(
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_min(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Fastest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_max(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Slowest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank <= 10) |>
    slice_max(weeks_on_chart, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Longest top-10 run")
) |>
  select(story, artist, track, song, first_rank, best_rank, first_best_week, weeks_on_chart)
```

###

Filtering to top-10 songs keeps the focus on recognizable hits while still leaving different stories to compare. Some hits peak quickly, some climb for months, and some last a long time without ever reaching number one.

### Exercise 13

Plot only the songs that reached the top 10. Show all top-10 songs in gray, then highlight the three notable songs from the previous exercise in color, with a legend showing their names. Render and inspect the plot in the rendered HTML.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Plot only the songs that reached the top 10. Show all top-10 songs in gray, then highlight the three notable songs from the previous exercise in color, with a legend showing their names. Render and inspect the plot in the rendered HTML. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: billboard-hot-100-11-answer
#| echo: true
billboard_longer <- billboard |>
  mutate(song = str_c(artist, " - ", track)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week))

billboard_song_summary <- billboard_longer |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  group_by(artist, track, song) |>
  summarise(
    best_rank = min(rank),
    first_best_week = min(week[rank == best_rank]),
    weeks_on_chart = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

billboard_top10_stories <- bind_rows(
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_min(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Fastest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_max(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Slowest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank <= 10) |>
    slice_max(weeks_on_chart, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Longest top-10 run")
)

billboard_top10_longer <- billboard_longer |>
  semi_join(
    billboard_song_summary |> filter(best_rank <= 10),
    by = c("artist", "track", "song")
  )

billboard_top10_longer |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = rank, group = song)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray75", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(
    data = billboard_top10_longer |>
      semi_join(billboard_top10_stories, by = c("artist", "track", "song")) |>
      filter(!is.na(rank)),
    aes(color = song),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = billboard_top10_stories,
    aes(x = first_best_week, y = best_rank, color = song),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = billboard_top10_stories,
    aes(
      x = first_best_week,
      y = best_rank,
      label = story,
      color = song
    ),
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 2.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "Top-10 hits follow different chart paths",
    subtitle = "Each line is one song that reached the top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100",
    x = "Weeks since entering the chart",
    y = "Billboard rank",
    color = "Song",
    caption = "Source: tidyr::billboard"
  )
```

###

The gray lines show the broader top-10 population; the colored lines turn three rows of the summary table into stories readers can follow. The three highlighted paths show that top-10 hits do not all follow the same shape: some reach number one quickly, some climb slowly, and some stay on the chart for many weeks without ever reaching the top.

###

Ranks are ordinal, not interval — the gap between #1 and #2 isn't the same as the gap between #50 and #51. The trajectory plot shows each song's *position* over time but not the *magnitude* of its popularity: two songs sitting at rank 50 in the same week could have had very different actual sales or airplay numbers.

## Summary

This tutorial used AI to analyze a year of Billboard Hot 100 rankings, drawing on [Chapter 7: Data Import](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html), [Chapter 5: Data Tidying](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html), and [Chapter 9: Layers](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html) of *R for Data Science (2e)*. You downloaded and parsed a CSV file, cached the parse so it runs once per change, reshaped the week columns into one row per song-week, found the cliff at week 20 and the chart rule behind it, and built a plot that highlights three notable hits against the rest of the top 10.

###

````{verbatim}
---
title: "Billboard Hot 100"
author: <your name>
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
billboard <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
billboard_longer <- billboard |>
  mutate(song = str_c(artist, " - ", track)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "rank"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week))

billboard_song_summary <- billboard_longer |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  group_by(artist, track, song) |>
  summarise(
    best_rank = min(rank),
    first_best_week = min(week[rank == best_rank]),
    weeks_on_chart = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

billboard_top10_stories <- bind_rows(
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_min(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Fastest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank == 1) |>
    slice_max(first_best_week, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Slowest to #1"),
  billboard_song_summary |>
    filter(best_rank <= 10) |>
    slice_max(weeks_on_chart, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(story = "Longest top-10 run")
)

billboard_top10_longer <- billboard_longer |>
  semi_join(
    billboard_song_summary |> filter(best_rank <= 10),
    by = c("artist", "track", "song")
  )

billboard_top10_longer |>
  filter(!is.na(rank)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = rank, group = song)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray75", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(
    data = billboard_top10_longer |>
      semi_join(billboard_top10_stories, by = c("artist", "track", "song")) |>
      filter(!is.na(rank)),
    aes(color = song),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = billboard_top10_stories,
    aes(x = first_best_week, y = best_rank, color = song),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = billboard_top10_stories,
    aes(
      x = first_best_week,
      y = best_rank,
      label = story,
      color = song
    ),
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 2.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(
    title = "Top-10 hits follow different chart paths",
    subtitle = "Each line is one song that reached the top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100",
    x = "Weeks since entering the chart",
    y = "Billboard rank",
    color = "Song",
    caption = "Source: tidyr::billboard"
  )
```
````

###

Your page now tells one story: how top-10 Billboard hits move through the chart, with three paths — Madonna's "Music" fastest to #1, Lonestar's "Amazed" slowest to #1, Creed's "Higher" with the longest run — called out by name.
